title: Salim Kumar Is on a Ventilator. The Man Who Made Malayalam Cinema Laugh Is Fighting for His Life.
excerpt: The National Award-winning actor, 56, has been rushed to a private hospital in Ernakulam. He had a liver transplant years ago and has been battling health issues since.
body:
Salim Kumar, one of Malayalam cinema's most beloved actors, has been admitted to a private hospital in Ernakulam and is currently on ventilator support. The 56-year-old National Award winner experienced health complications on Friday and was rushed into intensive care. No official medical bulletin has been released, but multiple reports confirm his condition is critical.

This is not the first time. Salim Kumar has been battling liver-related health issues for several years. He underwent a liver transplant in the past, and the complications from that procedure have shadowed his career and personal life ever since. He has spoken publicly about the toll it has taken, and has significantly reduced his workload during the 2020s because of it.

## From Mimicry Stages to National Recognition

Salim Kumar's career arc is one of the most extraordinary in Indian cinema. He did not come from a film family. He did not have industry connections. He started as a mimicry artist and stage performer, cutting his teeth at live shows across Kerala before getting a break in television through the comedy programme Comicola.

His film debut came in 1997 with Ishtamanu Nooru Vattam. But it was the early 2000s that turned him into a household name. A string of comedy films — Thenkasipattanam, Ee Parakkum Thalika, Meesa Madhavan, CID Moosa, Mayavi, Pulival Kalyanam, Chathikkatha Chanthu — made him one of the most recognisable faces in Malayalam cinema. His comic timing was not the loud, slapstick variety. It was rooted in character, in the absurd specificity of the people he played. His expressions, his pauses, his ability to deliver a punchline without appearing to try — these are the things that made audiences return to his films over and over.

But calling Salim Kumar a comedian sells him short. In 2010, he won the National Film Award for Best Actor — not in a comedy, but in the deeply moving Adaminte Makan Abu, directed by Salim Ahamed. The film told the story of an elderly Muslim couple saving money to go on the Hajj pilgrimage. Salim Kumar's performance was restrained, tender, and heartbreaking. It was the kind of award that does not just honour a performance but reframes an entire career.

He also won the Kerala State Film Award for Best Actor for Achanurangatha Veedu and the Kerala State Film Award for Best Story for his own directorial venture, Karutha Joothan. He directed three films in all — Compartment, Karutha Joothan, and Daivame Kaithozham K. Kumar Akanam — each one reflecting a sensibility that went far deeper than his on-screen comedy persona suggested.

## What Malayalam Cinema Owes Him

There is a generation of Malayali viewers — in Kerala, in the Gulf, in the US, in the UK, in Singapore — for whom Salim Kumar's films are foundational. His dialogues are memes before memes existed. His scenes from CID Moosa and Meesa Madhavan are quoted in family WhatsApp groups and college reunion chats. He is part of the cultural vocabulary of the Malayalam diaspora in a way that very few actors achieve.

His recent work has been limited by his health, but he has not stopped. He made a cameo appearance in Dileep's Bha Bha Ba and appeared in Sreenath Bhasi's Azadi. His son, Chandu Salim Kumar, has followed him into cinema, appearing in notable films including Malik and the blockbuster Manjummel Boys.

## The Waiting

For now, there is little to do but wait. The film fraternity in Kerala has expressed concern. Fans have flooded social media with prayers and memories of his best performances. The hospital has confirmed he is in the ICU under close observation. No further details have been shared.

What is clear is this: Salim Kumar is not just a comedian who won a National Award. He is an artist who understood that laughter and grief come from the same place. Malayalam cinema would not sound the same without him. It should not have to.
